title: Proteomic of Palmar Aponeurosis in Dupuytren`s Disease
summary:
Dupuytren's disease is a benign condition affecting the connective tissue in the hand. It causes changes in the tissue of the palm and fingers. The disease usually progresses slowly and, if left untreated, can lead to permanent bending of the fingers and a severe limitation of hand function. Both hands are often affected.
The condition is relatively common: about 9% of men and 3% of women are affected, mostly in older age.

The exact cause remains unclear to this day. There is evidence that various factors may play a role, such as smoking or genetic predisposition (i.e., inheritance within the family).

Pathological changes occur in the affected tissue: Certain proteins (collagen) are produced in increased amounts, and specialized cells (myofibroblasts) invade the tissue. This results in so-called nodules and cords that pull the fingers inward. In the palm, healthy and already altered areas often coexist side by side.

The diagnosis is usually made through a discussion with the patient (medical history) and a physical examination.

Depending on the extent of the condition, it is classified into different stages.
Conservative treatments such as splints or occupational therapy have proven to be of little effect. Therefore, surgical interventions are usually employed.

A major problem is that the disease often recurs after treatment—in some cases, very frequently. Subsequent surgeries are significantly more difficult,
time-consuming, and risky (e.g., due to nerve or vascular injuries). The recovery time afterward is also longer. That is why it is important to be able to better predict which patients are likely to experience a relapse.

The study presented here examines precisely this question.
To do so, a so-called proteomic analysis is being conducted. In this study, proteins in diseased tissue, healthy tissue, and blood are analyzed from patients with and without Dupuytren’s disease and compared with one another.

The aim is to determine whether there are differences between healthy and diseased tissue in the hand and whether patients with Dupuytren’s disease differ from healthy individuals. Are there changes in the blood associated with the disease? Can differences be identified between the initial onset and relapses?

In the long term, the goal is to determine whether the disease can be predicted early on and whether the risk of relapse can be better assessed.
In the best-case scenario, markers could even be found in the blood that indicate whether someone has an increased risk of Dupuytren’s disease or a relapse.

interventions.name:
The study aims to prospectively examine the proteome of blood and the palmar aponeurosis in 50 patients with primary Dupuytren’s disease (DD) and 25 with recurrent DD.
